tier_reason: The README gives the paper's headline result (up to 11.69x over llama.cpp, 13.20 tokens/s average and 29.08 peak on one RTX 4090), and WebSearch results list the same paper in ACM DL (DOI 10.1145/3694715.3695964) as SOSP '24, with the authors' copy named song-sosp24.pdf. The work is peer-reviewed, so B. It cannot be A: the README charts are images, no CPU model, compiler or flags are given, and the evaluation scripts (OPT code, predictor training) are listed as unreleased TODOs.

corrections.workload: Single-request LLM generation on one RTX 4090 (24 GB) with FP16 ReLU models (Falcon(ReLU)-40B, Llama(ReLU)-2-70B; the paper abstract also covers OPT-175B) at input length 64, plus an RTX 2080Ti (11 GB) run with INT4 ReLU models at input length 8. Speed is reported as end-to-end tokens/s (prompt + generation time divided by tokens generated).
corrections.caveats: The speedup depends on ReLU-sparsified models (ReLU/ReGLU/Squared-ReLU only). The README says standard llama.cpp weights run with no performance gain, and its FAQ admits the ReLU fine-tuned models (5B tokens of retraining) lose accuracy, especially the 70B. The llama.cpp baseline dates from late 2023. README charts are images, and the text gives only maxima (11x Falcon 40B, 3x Llama 2 70B on the 4090; 8x and 3x on the 2080Ti). The peer-reviewed paper (SOSP '24, DOI 10.1145/3694715.3695964) could not be opened from this container. CPU model, compiler and flags are not stated on pages opened. OPT support code and predictor-training code are still unreleased TODOs. The repo now lives at github.com/Tiiny-AI/PowerInfer (the SJTU-IPADS URL resolves there); Tiiny AI sells hardware built on it. It is derived from llama.cpp (LICENSE copyright Georgi Gerganov and SJTU-IPADS) but is not marked as a GitHub fork.

notes: Numbers match the README. Tier raised from C to B because the paper appeared at SOSP '24, but the venue was seen only in WebSearch result listings (arxiv.org, dl.acm.org and ipads.se.sjtu.edu.cn are blocked here); a retier check can confirm. The repo moved to Tiiny-AI/PowerInfer, so consider overriding repo_url. Metadata checked: MIT, 9.8k stars, last commit 2026-05-11, not archived, not a fork.

tier_reason: The only external comparison is a first-party chart (fully fused MLP vs TensorFlow 2.5.0 with XLA, RTX 3090) with no numbers in the text. Benchmark code is public at benchmarks/image/bench_ours.cu and benchmarks/image/bench_tensorflow.py, and CMake defaults to Release with --use_fast_math. CPU model, compiler and CUDA versions are not stated, so it is not A, and no peer-reviewed source could be opened, so it is not B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: The README chart (data/readme/fully-fused-vs-tensorflow.png) shows fully fused MLPs ahead of TensorFlow 2.5.0 with XLA at every batch size from 2^14 to 2^21 on an RTX 3090. Read from the chart (approximate, derived from page data), 64-neuron-wide training throughput is about 1.2e8 vs 0.12e8 elements/s at batch 2^14 (~10x), narrowing to about 2.0e8 vs 1.0e8 at 2^21 (~2x). 64-wide inference is about 1.08e9 vs 0.14e9 elements/s at 2^21 (~8x), with a larger gap at small batches. The 128-wide (dashed) gap is about 2x to 6x for training. Separately, the README claims JIT fusion gives 1.5x to 2.5x over tiny-cuda-nn's own earlier path (it can slow down RTX 3000-series or large models), and Instant NGP gets 5x by fusing its NeRF ray marcher into one kernel.
corrections.caveats: The TensorFlow comparison is a chart with no numbers in the text, against a 2021 TensorFlow 2.5 plus XLA baseline. The README names benchmarks/bench_ours.cu and benchmarks/bench_tensorflow.py, but those paths 404; the files now live at benchmarks/image/bench_ours.cu and benchmarks/image/bench_tensorflow.py (an image-learning workload). CPU model, compiler and CUDA versions are not stated; the CMake defaults are Release and --use_fast_math. The 1.5x-2.5x and 5x figures are against the library's own earlier path or a non-fused application, not an external baseline. The fully fused MLP paper (Mueller et al. 2021, real-time neural radiance caching) could not be opened (tom94.net is blocked here).

notes: Metadata checked: BSD-3-Clause, 4.5k stars, last commit 2026-09-29, not archived, not a fork. The chart values were read from the PNG and are approximate.

tier_reason: First-party tables in docs/benchmarks/benchmarks.md compare ZhiLight against vLLM and SGLang, with exact launch arguments for each engine. The benchmark tool ships only as a Docker image (ghcr.io/zhihu/zhilight/benchmark), engine versions are not stated, and no CPU model, compiler or flags are given, so C.

corrections.workload: LLM serving benchmark (QPS, TTFT, TPOT) with 3.7k-token prompts (DeepSeek-R1 AWQ: 2.8k prompt, 750 output tokens) on NVIDIA AD102 PCIe (x1, x2, x4), A800 (x4, x8) and H20 (x8), for models from MiniCPM-2B to DeepSeek-R1. Runs use the ZhiLight benchmark Docker tool, which sweeps offered QPS via --min_qps/--max_qps/--qps_step.
corrections.caveats: Results are mixed within the same document. Llama-3.1-8B on 2x AD102: ZhiLight QPS 0.4 vs vLLM 0.46 and SGLang 0.84, TTFT 1091.12 vs 915.58 ms (vLLM), TPOT 66.24 vs 18.68 ms (vLLM). Qwen2-72B on 4x A800: SGLang QPS 0.36 vs ZhiLight 0.18. Qwen1.5-110B on 4x A800: SGLang QPS 0.18 vs ZhiLight 0.1. ZhiLight TPOT is worse in several rows (DeepSeek-R1 AWQ 115.97 vs vLLM 109.86 ms; Qwen1.5-110B on AD102 39.68 vs 30.34 ms; MiniCPM-2B 26.1 vs 16.71 ms). The clearest wins are TTFT on PCIe AD102 multi-GPU runs. QPS values look like offered-load steps from the benchmark tool (many engines tie at exactly 0.09 or 0.18), so QPS ratios may reflect the highest load step sustained rather than measured throughput. The benchmark tool is distributed as a Docker image, with its source not found in the pages opened. vLLM/SGLang versions and compiler flags are not stated, and there is no H20 baseline. This is an LLM serving engine rather than a kernel library, and its baselines are not in the category list.
